—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

CISA KEV: CVE-2026-48558 — SimpleHelp Authentication Bypass Vulnerability

CISA KEV
2026-06-29 1 use case 0 techniques 2 kill-chain phases detected

SimpleHelp contains an authentication bypass vulnerability in the OIDC authentication flow. When OIDC authentication is configured, identity tokens submitted during login are accepted without verifying their cryptographic signature. In a vulnerable configuration, a remote, unauthenticated attacker can submit a forged token containing arbitrary identity claims to obtain a fully authenticated technician session. In some configurations, this may also allow bypass of multi-factor authentication. Vendor: SimpleHelp , Product: SimpleHelp. Federal patch due: 2026-07-02.

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "4a8860240e4231c3a74c81949be655a28e096a7d72f38fbe84e5b37636b98417", "ae70dd4f6bc0d1c8c2848e4e6b51934626c4818dcb5af99d080ddbd7dc337185", "2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Threat Brief: Mitigating Large-Scale Credential Attacks

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)
2026-06-26 11 use cases 2 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

We provide guidance for preparing for and mitigating large-scale credential attacks, focusing on recent campaigns targeting security vendors' devices. The post Threat Brief: Mitigating Large-Scale Credential Attacks appeared first on Unit 42 .

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] FortiBleed password-spray success burst against internet-facing Fortinet/edge auth · [LLM] FortiGate jsconsole / loopback admin login (CVE-2024-55591 auth-bypass exploitation) · [LLM] FortiBleed MSSQL login-failure burst then success (internet-exposed SQL spraying) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] FortiGate rogue super_admin / SSL-VPN account creation following CVE-2024-55591 exploit · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
FortiBleed password-spray success burst against internet-facing Fortinet/edge auth AIExploitation Medium
Hunts a single source IP producing a high volume of failed authentications against a Fortinet appliance (SSL-VPN / admin login) followed by a successful login in the same window — the exact 'successful logins shortly after large-volume password failure events' pattern Unit 42 flags for the FortiBleed credential-spraying campaign. Rationale: Implements Unit 42's explicit FortiBleed guidance — audit remote-access logs for successful logins shortly after large-volume failure events — scoped to Fortinet auth via the CIM app values / DeviceVendor='Fortinet'. Threshold + same-window success join is what separates spray-then-compromise from routine VPN typos. Cross-checked with SOCRadar/SecurityWeek FortiBleed reporting and Arctic Wolf's CVE-2024-55591 analysis. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/what-is-fortibleed/ • https://www.securityweek.com/fortibleed-86000-fortinet-device-credentials-compromised/ • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/cve-2024-55591/
ATT&CKT1110.003 T1110.004 T1133
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate remote worker repeatedly fat-fingering an SSL-VPN password then succeeding
  • Misconfigured VPN client or saved-credential loop retrying stale creds before a successful re-auth
  • Authenticated vulnerability scanner (Qualys/Tenable) credential checks against the appliance
  • Shared NAT egress IP where many staff log in (inflated failure+success counts from one SourceIP)
  • Password-rotation day causing widespread first-attempt failures followed by success
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<populate watchlist: known scanner + corp NAT egress IPs via a Sentinel watchlist join, not inline>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the CompromisedUser + SourceIP; geolocate SourceIP and check whether the success used MFA and from a known ASN/country. Inspect the failed-user set — many distinct users from one IP = spray, not a typo. 2) Contain: if SourceIP is foreign/unrecognized, force-disable the compromised admin/VPN account, kill active SSL-VPN tunnels, block the SourceIP at the edge, and rotate the credential. 3) Hunt: from that SourceIP/account pivot to post-auth config changes (new admin accounts, sslvpn user groups), jsconsole admin logins, and any config download — feed into the FortiBleed jsconsole and rogue-admin UCs.
let lookback = 7d;
let window = 1h;
let Failed = CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where Activity has "login" and (EventOutcome in~ ("failure","failed") or Message has_any ("login failed","Login failed","authentication failed","ssl-login-fail"))
| summarize Failures = count(), TargetUsers = dcount(DestinationHostName) by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, window);
let Success = CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where Activity has "login" and (EventOutcome in~ ("success","succeeded") or Message has_any ("login successful","SSL tunnel established"))
| summarize Successes = count(), CompromisedUser = make_set(DestinationHostName, 20) by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, window);
Failed
| where Failures >= 30   // 30 = empirical spray burst floor per source per hour
| join kind=inner Success on SourceIP, TimeGenerated
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, Failures, TargetUsers, Successes, CompromisedUser
| order by Failures desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| stats sum(eval(if(action="failure",count,0))) as failures, sum(eval(if(action="success",count,0))) as successes, dc(user) as targeted_users, values(eval(if(action="success",user,null()))) as compromised_user, values(dest) as dest by src, _time
| where failures >= 30 and successes >= 1
| sort - failures
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app IN ("fortios","fortigate","fortiproxy","ftnt-fortigate","sslvpn-plain","forticlient_ems") by Authentication.src, Authentication.dest, Authentication.user, Authentication.action, _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| stats sum(eval(if(action="failure",count,0))) as failures, sum(eval(if(action="success",count,0))) as successes, dc(user) as targeted_users, values(eval(if(action="success",user,null()))) as compromised_user, values(dest) as dest by src, _time
| where failures >= 30 and successes >= 1
| sort - failures
FortiGate jsconsole / loopback admin login (CVE-2024-55591 auth-bypass exploitation) AIExploitation High
Hunts the high-fidelity exploitation signature of CVE-2024-55591: administrative logins attributed to the 'jsconsole' interface and/or successful super-admin logins sourced from the device loopback/local IP — the artifact the Node.js websocket auth-bypass leaves when an unauthenticated attacker forges super_admin access on FortiOS/FortiProxy. Rationale: Uses the two corroborated CVE-2024-55591 exploitation artifacts — `ui=jsconsole` in the admin-login record (matched in CommonSecurityLog Message) and super-admin logins from the device loopback/local IP (CIM Authentication.src=127.0.0.1) — reported by Arctic Wolf, watchTowr ('I Am The Super_Admin Now') and Trustwave. Both are near-zero in benign FortiGate operation. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/cve-2024-55591/ • https://labs.watchtowr.com/get-fortirekt-i-am-the-super_admin-now-fortios-authentication-bypass-cve-2024-55591/ • https://trustwave.com/en-us/resources/blogs/spiderlabs-blog/cve-2024-55591-fortinet-fortios-fortiproxy-zero-day
ATT&CKT1190 T1078.001 T1556
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin legitimately running CLI commands through the FortiGate GUI 'CLI console' widget (also tagged jsconsole) — distinguish by source being a real admin IP, not loopback
  • Automation/orchestration tooling (Ansible/FortiManager) driving CLI via the local console
  • Internal penetration test replicating CVE-2024-55591
  • Health-check scripts hitting the management interface from a jump host
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the jsconsole/loopback login corresponds to a real admin session — legitimate jsconsole use originates from an authenticated GUI session with a genuine admin SourceIP; exploitation shows loopback/local src and no preceding interactive auth. Check FortiOS version against the CVE-2024-55591 fixed builds. 2) Contain: isolate the device's management interface from the internet, disable/rotate all admin accounts, and capture the running + startup config for IR. 3) Hunt: enumerate admin accounts and sslvpn user groups created/modified after the first jsconsole login, look for `--userfrom`-style audit-record tampering, and any config download/exfil to chain with the rogue-admin and FortiBleed config-extraction UCs.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where Message has "jsconsole"
| where Message has_any ("login","logged in","logged-in","admin")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceProduct, DeviceExternalID, SourceIP, AdminUser = SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, Activity, EventOutcome, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| `ctime(firstTime)` | `ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - firstTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime, values(Authentication.dest) as dest from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=success Authentication.app IN ("fortios","fortigate","fortiproxy","ftnt-fortigate") (Authentication.src="127.0.0.1" OR Authentication.src="0.0.0.0" OR Authentication.src="::1") by Authentication.user, Authentication.src
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`

| sort - firstTime
FortiGate rogue super_admin / SSL-VPN account creation following CVE-2024-55591 exploit AIInstallation High
Hunts post-exploitation persistence for the FortiBleed/CVE-2024-55591 chain: creation of new FortiGate administrator accounts (often random usernames) or new SSL-VPN local users / user groups via config changes. This is how attackers convert a one-shot auth bypass into durable, high-privilege access for offline-cracked credential re-use. Rationale: Targets the documented CVE-2024-55591 post-exploit actions — new admin accounts with random names, new SSL-VPN local users and groups — via Fortinet config-change logs (cfgpath system.admin / user.group) and the CIM Change datamodel (action=created, object_category=user). Account creation on an edge appliance is rare and tightly change-controlled, so FP is low. Corroborated by Arctic Wolf and Cyble. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/cve-2024-55591/ • https://cyble.com/blog/cve-2024-55591-the-fortinet-flaw-putting-critical-systems-at-risk/
ATT&CKT1136 T1098 T1133
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Planned admin onboarding by the network team during a change window
  • FortiManager/automation pushing a config template that provisions admin or VPN users
  • Legitimate SSL-VPN user-group expansion during an access-request rollout
  • MSP/managed-SOC provisioning a monitoring admin account
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the ActorAdmin and SourceIP that created the new object; correlate against an authorized change ticket and verify the actor session was not a jsconsole/loopback exploit login. Flag random-looking usernames. 2) Contain: delete or disable the unauthorized admin/VPN account and group, terminate its sessions, and rotate credentials for every legitimate admin on the device. 3) Hunt: review whether the new account granted VPN access, established tunnels into internal networks, or downloaded the device config; pivot on its SourceIP across other edge devices to scope the FortiBleed campaign footprint.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where Message has_any ("system.admin","user.local","user.group")
| where Message has_any ("super_admin","prof_admin","accprofile","sslvpn")
| where Message has_any ("Object attribute configured","Added","cfgattr","New","create")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, ActorAdmin = SourceUserName, NewObject = DestinationHostName, Activity, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, min(_time) as firstTime, values(All_Changes.user) as actor, values(All_Changes.command) as command from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.action=created All_Changes.object_category=user All_Changes.vendor_product IN ("Fortinet FortiGate","FortiGate","FortiOS","Fortinet FortiProxy") by All_Changes.dest, All_Changes.object
| `drop_dm_object_name(Change)`
| `ctime(firstTime)`
| sort - firstTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count, min(_time) as firstTime, values(All_Changes.user) as actor, values(All_Changes.command) as command from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.action=created All_Changes.object_category=user All_Changes.vendor_product IN ("Fortinet FortiGate","FortiGate","FortiOS","Fortinet FortiProxy") by All_Changes.dest, All_Changes.object
| `drop_dm_object_name(Change)`
| `ctime(firstTime)`
| sort - firstTime
FortiBleed MSSQL login-failure burst then success (internet-exposed SQL spraying) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the FortiBleed campaign's parallel targeting of internet-exposed MSSQL: a single client IP generating a burst of SQL Server login failures (error 18456) across one or many logins within a short window — the spray signature Unit 42 observed against MSSQL devices alongside Fortinet and Sophos. Rationale: Covers the article's explicit observation that the FortiBleed actors also targeted MSSQL devices. Pivots on SQL Server error 18456 (login failed) parsed for CLIENT IP and login name in Sentinel's Event table, with a Defender DeviceLogonEvents fallback for Windows-auth brute force against the SQL host and a CIM Authentication path for Splunk. Threshold-based, so framed as a burst detector. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/what-is-fortibleed/ • https://www.securityweek.com/fortibleed-86000-fortinet-device-credentials-compromised/
ATT&CKT1110.003 T1078
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Application/service account with a stale connection string hammering the DB after a password change
  • Linked-server or ETL job misconfigured with wrong credentials retrying in a tight loop
  • Monitoring agent (SCOM/SolarWinds) probing SQL with expired creds
  • Authenticated vulnerability scanner credential audit against the SQL instance
  • Developer load-test pointing at the wrong SQL host
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !in~ ("sqlmonitor","svc-etl","svc-backup")   // tune to your known SQL service accounts
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve ClientIP — internal app server vs external/unknown. Inspect the targeted login set: many distinct logins from one IP = spray; a single service account = likely stale credential. Check for any 18454/successful login from the same ClientIP right after the burst. 2) Contain: if external, block the ClientIP at the firewall, confirm the SQL instance is not directly internet-exposed, and disable SQL-auth logins that were sprayed; enforce that MSSQL sits behind the VPN/jump box. 3) Hunt: if a success followed, review that login's subsequent activity (xp_cmdshell, new SQL logins, linked-server abuse) and pivot the ClientIP across Fortinet edge logs to tie it to the broader FortiBleed spraying infrastructure.
DeviceLogonEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "LogonFailed"
| where LogonType in ("Network","Batch")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize Failures = count(), TargetedAccounts = dcount(AccountName), Accounts = make_set(AccountName, 30), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by RemoteIP, DeviceName, bin(Timestamp, 30m)
| where Failures >= 30   // 30 failed network logons / 30 min from one source = spray
| order by Failures desc
let lookback = 7d;
let window = 30m;
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where Source == "MSSQLSERVER"
| where EventID == 18456   // SQL Server: Login failed
| extend LoginUser = extract(@"Login failed for user '([^']+)'", 1, RenderedDescription)
| extend ClientIP = extract(@"\[CLIENT: ([0-9A-Fa-f\.:]+)\]", 1, RenderedDescription)
| where isnotempty(ClientIP)
| summarize Failures = count(), TargetedLogins = dcount(LoginUser), Logins = make_set(LoginUser, 30) by ClientIP, Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, window)
| where Failures >= 30
| order by Failures desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",

| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:

      article before alerting.
level: medium

        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("flipboxstudio.info")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]
High

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Gamaredon HTA downloader auto-executing from Startup folder at logon (mshta.exe) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Gamaredon WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 ADS path-traversal dropping HTA/VBS into Startup folder · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Gamaredon dead-drop C&C resolution via Telegra.ph and GoFile from script hosts · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Gamaredon stealer exfiltration to S3-compatible cloud storage (Wasabi/Tebi/Intercolo) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Gamaredon WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 ADS path-traversal dropping HTA/VBS into Startup folder AIInstallation High
Hunts the persistence step Gamaredon adopted from 2025-09-26: a malicious RAR archive exploiting WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 (alternate-data-stream path traversal) to write an HTA/VBS/VBE/LNK downloader into the user's Startup folder so it auto-runs at next login. Article-specific because it pins the writing process to WinRAR-family binaries and the target to the Startup directory. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete persistence pivot (CVE-2025-8088 → HTA/VBS into Startup folder, active from 2025-09-26) and the WinRAR extraction binaries; Mandiant/Google and SOC Prime confirm the same ADS-to-Startup write pattern (.hta/.vbs/.vbe) across multiple Russia-aligned actors, so it is second-sourced. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/exploiting-critical-winrar-vulnerability • https://socprime.com/active-threats/cve-2025-8088-critical-winrar-vulnerability/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/winrar-path-traversal-flaw-still-exploited-by-numerous-hackers/amp/
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1203 T1564.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate installers shipped as RAR self-extractors that legitimately add a startup launcher
  • IT-deployed login scripts (.vbs/.lnk) packaged in archives by an admin
  • Software that bundles an updater shortcut into Startup after archive extraction
  • Security/portable apps extracted with WinRAR that create a startup auto-run by design
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/sfx","setup","install") and InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the dropped file's full path/hash and the parent RAR archive; detonate or read the HTA/VBS content for a download URL and confirm WinRAR version < 7.13 on the host. 2) Contain: delete/quarantine the Startup-folder artifact, isolate the host before next logon (the payload fires at login), and block any URLs/domains found in the script. 3) Hunt: search the org for the same archive SHA256 in mail/download telemetry, for other hosts running unpatched WinRAR, and for follow-on mshta/wscript execution and connections to telegra.ph / gofile.io / S3 storage domains.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\"
| where FileName endswith ".hta" or FileName endswith ".vbs" or FileName endswith ".vbe" or FileName endswith ".lnk"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("winrar.exe","rar.exe","unrar.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("winrar.exe","rar.exe","unrar.exe")
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\"
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("hta","vbs","vbe","lnk")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 Script Drop into Startup Folder
id: a3f8c1d2-4b6e-4f21-9c7a-1e2d3f4a5b6c
description: Detects WinRAR-family process writing an HTA/VBS/VBE/LNK file into the user Startup folder, consistent with CVE-2025-8088 path-traversal persistence used by Gamaredon in 2025.
references:
  - https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/gamaredon-2025-leveraging-tunnels-workers-dead-drops-new-alliances/

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/26
tags:

  - attack.t1203

logsource:
  category: file_event

detection:
  selection_proc:

      - '\winrar.exe'
      - '\rar.exe'
      - '\unrar.exe'

  condition: selection_proc and selection_path and selection_ext
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\WinRAR.exe OR *\winrar.exe OR *\Rar.exe OR *\rar.exe OR *\UnRAR.exe OR *\unrar.exe) @TargetFilename:(*\Startup\*.hta OR *\Startup\*.vbs OR *\Startup\*.vbe OR *\Startup\*.lnk)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| ContextImageFileName=/\\(winrar|rar|unrar)\.exe$/i
| TargetFileName=/\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\.+\.(hta|vbs|vbe|lnk)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\*") AND (Filesystem.file_name="*.hta" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.vbs" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.vbe" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.lnk") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | search process_name IN ("winrar.exe","rar.exe","unrar.exe") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Gamaredon HTA downloader auto-executing from Startup folder at logon (mshta.exe) AIExploitation High
Hunts execution of the persisted Gamaredon HTA downloader: mshta.exe launched at user logon with a command line referencing an .hta inside the Startup folder. Complements the file-write detection by catching execution even when the original drop was missed. Rationale: Pins to the article's specific persistence-to-execution chain (HTA downloader placed in Startup executes at next login) and the LOLBin mshta with a Startup-path command line, a combination with near-zero legitimate occurrence; corroborated by Google/Mandiant noting HTA-in-Startup as the second-stage downloader. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/exploiting-critical-winrar-vulnerability
ATT&CKT1218.005 T1547.001 T1059.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legacy in-house HTA-based dashboard intentionally placed in Startup by IT
  • Vendor application that uses an HTA splash/launcher auto-started at logon
  • Admin troubleshooting that temporarily drops an HTA in Startup
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the mshta command line and the referenced .hta path; read the HTA body for embedded URLs/next-stage (PteroSand VBScript) and check whether a RAR/CVE-2025-8088 drop preceded it. 2) Contain: kill the mshta process, remove the Startup artifact, isolate the host, and block extracted C2/dead-drop domains. 3) Hunt: pivot on the user/host for child wscript/cscript execution, temporary .vbs written-then-deleted (PteroDum), and egress to telegra.ph, gofile.io, or S3 storage providers.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "mshta.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\"
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".hta"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "mshta.exe"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has ".hta"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Gamaredon stealer exfiltration to S3-compatible cloud storage (Wasabi/Tebi/Intercolo) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts PteroVDoor/PteroPSDoor's 2025 primary exfiltration channel: scripted upload of stolen files to S3-compatible storage at wasabisys.com, tebi.io, or i3storage.com (Intercolo de-fra.i3storage.com) initiated by a script host rather than a browser. High-fidelity because exfil from wscript/powershell/mshta to these specific providers is anomalous. Rationale: Uses the corroborated exfil endpoints (Wasabi=wasabisys.com, Tebi=tebi.io, Intercolo=de-fra.i3storage.com) named as Gamaredon's 2025 primary exfil channel, scoped to script-host initiators to suppress normal browser/backup S3 traffic; ESET's own write-up and the search-confirmed config-rotation (Wasabi→Tebi→Intercolo) second-source the domains. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/gamaredon-2025-leveraging-tunnels-workers-dead-drops-new-alliances/ • https://www.govinfosecurity.com/russias-gamaredon-adapts-tactics-to-target-ukraine-a-32068
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1059.001 T1059.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Corporate backup/sync software legitimately using Wasabi S3 (but normally via its own binary, not wscript/powershell)
  • Developer/DevOps PowerShell scripts pushing artifacts to a sanctioned Wasabi/Tebi bucket
  • A red-team or admin ad-hoc PowerShell aws/s3 upload
  • Telemetry where a browser helper is misattributed as the initiating process
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("aws s3","Backup","veeam") and InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("backupsvc","svc-backup"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating script host, its command line, and the volume/bytes uploaded; confirm the bucket/host is not a sanctioned corporate storage account. 2) Contain: block the storage FQDNs at the proxy/firewall, isolate the host, and preserve the stealer binary/script for analysis. 3) Hunt: trace back to the persistence/execution chain (mshta-from-Startup, WinRAR drop), enumerate which files were staged/read prior to upload, and sweep other hosts for DNS to the same three providers.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("wasabisys.com","tebi.io","i3storage.com")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","cmd.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("wasabisys.com","tebi.io","i3storage.com")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Gamaredon dead-drop C&C resolution via Telegra.ph and GoFile from script hosts AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts PteroOdd (Telegra.ph API) and PteroEffigy (GoFile) fetching next-stage payloads / resolving C&C from legitimate dead-drop services, requested by a Windows script host. Article-specific because it targets the exact two services named for these downloaders rather than generic LOLBin egress. Rationale: Targets the two specific dead-drop services the article ties to named downloaders (PteroOdd→Telegra.ph API, PteroEffigy→GoFile) and scopes to script-host initiators so normal browser visits to telegra.ph/gofile are excluded; flagged Medium because only the original ESET piece names these two services for these tools. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/gamaredon-2025-leveraging-tunnels-workers-dead-drops-new-alliances/
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1105 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user legitimately downloading a shared file from gofile.io that an EDR attributes to a script wrapper
  • Automation/scripts that scrape telegra.ph articles for benign content
  • Browser child processes mis-tagged as the initiating process
  • Security tooling sandboxing a URL that resolves these domains
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the script-host command line and the full URL/telegra.ph path or gofile content ID; pull what was downloaded and decode any retrieved next-stage C&C address. 2) Contain: block telegra.ph/gofile.io egress from the host, isolate it, and add the resolved real C&C to blocklists. 3) Hunt: correlate with preceding HTA/mshta execution and following uploads to wasabisys.com/tebi.io/i3storage.com on the same host, and sweep the org for other script hosts touching these dead-drop services.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("telegra.ph","gofile.io")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","cmd.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("telegra.ph","gofile.io")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc

| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-8088")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-8088")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2025-8088")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2025-8088")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host

Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
